title: Arrays and the loops that fit them
summary: Indexed and associative arrays, foreach with keys, and the functions that fit them.

blocks.html: An array is an ordered table of key and value pairs. In the common case you leave the keys out: ["John", "Jane", "Maria"] gets the keys 0, 1, 2 in the order you wrote them. array(...) is the older spelling of the same literal and still appears in existing code.

blocks.title: an indexed array
blocks.code:
<?php

$persons = ["John", "Jane", "Maria"];
$cars = array("Toyota", "Honda", "Ford");   // same array, older spelling

echo $persons[0], "\n";
echo $persons[2], "\n";
echo count($cars), " cars\n";

blocks.html: $persons[] = "Pedro"; appends at the next free index. You may also write a key yourself, and then the keys can have gaps: start with two names, append one, then assign index 10, and count() reports 4 — it counts elements, not the highest key.

blocks.title: appending, and gaps
blocks.code:
<?php

$persons = ["John", "Jane"];

$persons[] = "Maria";      // next free index, 2
$persons[10] = "Pedro";    // a gap is allowed; the key stays 10

echo count($persons), "\n";
echo $persons[2], "\n";
echo $persons[10], "\n";

blocks.html: The shape you will use every day is the associative array: string keys that describe the value, so the code reads like the thing it represents. A record is one array, and a list of records is an array of arrays.

blocks.title: string keys, and reading them with foreach
blocks.code:
<?php

$student = [
    "Student ID" => 1001,
    "Student Name" => "Juan Dela Cruz",
    "Course" => "BSIT",
];

echo $student["Student Name"], "\n";

foreach ($student as $key => $value) {
    echo $key, ": ", $value, "\n";
}
blocks.output:
Juan Dela Cruz
Student ID: 1001
Student Name: Juan Dela Cruz
Course: BSIT

blocks.title: what an array actually is
blocks.ascii:
$student
    key             value
    "Student ID"    1001
    "Student Name"  "Juan Dela Cruz"
    "Course"        "BSIT"

  An indexed array is the same table with 0, 1, 2 as keys,
  in the order the values were written.

blocks.title: an array of records
blocks.code:
<?php

$students = [
    ["Student ID" => 1001, "Student Name" => "Juan Dela Cruz"],
    ["Student ID" => 1002, "Student Name" => "Maria Santos"],
];

foreach ($students as $student) {
    echo $student["Student ID"], " - ", $student["Student Name"], "\n";
}

blocks.title: four functions that save a loop
blocks.code:
<?php

$names = ["juan", "maria", "pedro"];
$scores = [80, 95, 0, 71];

// implode() glues an array back into one string
echo implode(", ", array_map('strtoupper', $names)), "\n";
echo array_sum($scores), "\n";
echo implode(", ", array_filter($scores)), "\n";   // without a callback: drops falsy
var_dump(in_array(95, $scores));

blocks.title: keys, sort and usort
blocks.code:
<?php

$scores = ["quiz" => 80, "final" => 95, "midterm" => 71];
echo implode(", ", array_keys($scores)), "\n";

$names = ["Maria", "juan", "Pedro"];
sort($names);                      // ASCII order: capitals first
sort($scores);                     // keys are gone: now 0, 1, 2
echo implode(", ", $names), "\n";
echo implode(", ", $scores), "\n";

$names = ["Maria", "juan", "Pedro"];
usort($names, 'strcasecmp');       // your own comparison, case-insensitive
echo implode(", ", $names), "\n";
blocks.output:
quiz, final, midterm
Maria, Pedro, juan
71, 80, 95
juan, Maria, Pedro

blocks.html:
sort() sorts values and reindexes, which is why it is the wrong tool for a table with meaningful keys. usort() takes the comparison as an argument, so it can sort records any way you want — the usual form passes a small anonymous function, and chapter 06 shows you how to write those. Here a built-in comparison does the job.

That is everything public/student_directory_with_functions_array.php needs. Its $students array is the two-element table you just built, plus a third student, and it hands the table to displayStudents().

quiz.q: You append to ["a", "b"] with $list[] = "c". Which key does the new element get?
quiz.why: The next free numeric index is used, so the third element gets 2. Existing keys are never reused, even if earlier ones were removed.

quiz.q: What does array_filter($scores) do when you pass no callback?
quiz.why: Without a callback the current value is tested for truthiness, so 0, "0", "", null and [] all disappear. A zero score silently vanishing is a real bug.

quiz.q: Why is sort() the wrong choice for ["quiz" => 80, "final" => 95]?
options: It sorts and reindexes, losing the keys
quiz.why: sort() rebuilds the array with keys 0 and 1, so the labels quiz and final are gone. asort() and ksort() are the ones that keep keys.

exercise.brief: Build the students table from the directory page (Juan 1001, Maria 1002, Pedro 1003). Print one line per student as 1001 - Juan Dela Cruz, then a final line Total: 3.
exercise.starter:
<?php

// an array of records, then one line each, then the total
exercise.hint: Each record is ["Student ID" => 1001, "Student Name" => "Juan Dela Cruz"]. Use foreach over the outer array and count($students) for the total.
exercise.solution:
<?php

$students = [
    ["Student ID" => 1001, "Student Name" => "Juan Dela Cruz"],
    ["Student ID" => 1002, "Student Name" => "Maria Santos"],
    ["Student ID" => 1003, "Student Name" => "Pedro Reyes"],
];

foreach ($students as $student) {
    echo $student["Student ID"], " - ", $student["Student Name"], "\n";
}

echo "Total: ", count($students), "\n";
